newsitem.title: USA: Senate easily approves balanced budget measure.
newsitem.headline: Senate easily approves balanced budget measure.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday approved bipartisan legislation designed to balance the budget and shrink the size of the federal government, sending the measure to President Bill Clinton for his promised signature.

Capping months of tough negotiations and heated political rhetoric, the Senate quickly passed the measure by a lopsided vote of 85-15. It then opened debate on a companion measure cutting taxes by a net $95 billion over five years.
The House, which passed the budget bill on Wednesday, is also considering the tax bill, which leaders hope to send to the White House by Friday.

"On both sides of the aisle and both ends of Pennsylvania Avenue, Republicans and Democrats, House and Senate and, yes, the president are all saying, 'This is good for America,'" said Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott. "It's a major step forward. Maybe not a leap, but a major step."
The victory was particularly sweet for Republicans who have long made balancing the budget a top political priority.
That goal appeared out of reach in 1995 when Republicans forced an unpopular government shutdown in a failed effort to get Clinton to agree to a more sweeping budget plan.

The White House and Republians this year decided a deal was a political imperative. Helped along by a booming economy, they agreed on a five-year spending and tax pact that is supposed to erase the deficit by 2002.

Clinton, who won significant new spending initiatives while agreeing to deep cuts in Medicare, hailed approval of the budget bill as, "the achievement of a generation and a triumph for every American."
"This budget marks an end to decades of deficits and just as important, it honours our values," he said in a statement.
Vice President Al Gore, in his role as presiding officer of the Senate, announced the final vote to the chamber. Twelve of the Senate's 55 Republicans voted no, along with three of its 45 Democrats.

Conservatives, like Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm, complained the legislation did not go nearly far enough to rein in long-term entitlement costs, while creating an expensive new children's health plan, budgeted at $24 billion.
"It has already grown to $24 billion before we adopt the bill. Does anybody believe this programme is not going to explode in the future?" Gramm said.
On the other hand, Democratic opponents groused the measure went too far, cutting Medicare and other social programmes in order to fund a package of tax cuts that would mainly benefit the well-off.
Some lawmakers voted against the bill because it included a 15-cents-per-pack increase in the fedearl cigarette tax.
Despite the rhetoric, the legislation approved Thursday by itself would not bring the budget into balance.
It cuts spending on mandatory programmes such as Medicare and Medicaid by about $130 billion over five years.
Congress was directed to find another $140 billion in reductions over that same period as part of annual spending bills, but the measure did not say where they come from.
Critics charged future Congresses will never muster the political will to cut veterans, education, nutrition and other social programmes, making the bill an empty promise.
The legislation reduces Medicare by about $115 billion over five years, largely by cutting payments to hospitals, managed care and other health providers.

Beneficiaries would see monthly premiums rise to $67 in 2002 from $43.80 this year. They would have an expanded menu of preventive benefits and more insurance choices -- including tax-free medical savings accounts opposed by the White House.

Lawmakers delivered a new $24 billion programme of grants for states to expand health care to the nation's 10 million uninsured children. The programme would be funded partly through a 15 cents-per-pack cigarette tax rise.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates the plan will cover about two million previously uninsured children.
The White House won welfare spending, restoring aid to hundreds of thousands of legal immigrants, creating a $3 billion welfare-to-work programme and easing Food Stamp cuts.
Medicaid insurance for the poor, elderly and disabled would fall by more than $13 billion. Most of the savings come from trimming aid to hospitals serving indigent patients.
The measure includes reductions in nutrition and education programmes and calls on regulators to auction off part of the public broadcast spectrum, raising $21 billion.
